title: Canary-Controlled Safe-Data Interleaving for Reducing Emergent Misalignment

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to mitigate emergent misalignment (EM) during fine-tuning by dynamically adjusting defense strength based on the model's real-time risk state, rather than using fixed interleaving ratios. Several prior papers address emergent misalignment, but none propose or pursue the specific objective of dynamically adjusting defense strength in response to real-time risk. For example, [1], [2], [5], and [7] focus on understanding, preventing, or mitigating EM, but they do so through static mechanisms (e.g., latent blocking in [2] or dataset-level interventions in [5]) rather than dynamic, real-time adjustments. No prior paper explicitly targets the same purpose of adaptive, risk-sensitive mitigation.

### Mechanism
The mechanism is a closed-loop adaptive interleaving framework that uses canary prompts to compute an EMA-smoothed risk estimate and adjusts the safe-data interleaving ratio via a threshold-based policy with hysteresis. While [13] and [15] describe interleaving-based control frameworks in unrelated domains (e.g., vehicle stability and optimal control), these mechanisms are not substantively equivalent because they do not involve canary-controlled risk estimation or adaptive interleaving for LLM safety. Similarly, [16] uses canaries for exploitability evaluation in binary programs, but this is unrelated to adaptive interleaving or fine-tuning alignment. No prior paper combines these elements into a substantively equivalent mechanism.

### Evaluation
The evaluation uses the Security EM benchmark with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct to measure General %Misaligned under different interleaving strategies. While the specific benchmark instance (Security EM) and model (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) are new, the evaluation design — measuring misalignment rates under different fine-tuning strategies — is not novel. For example, [1], [5], and [10] evaluate misalignment rates across various fine-tuning setups, and [6] specifically evaluates Qwen-2.5 models for resistance to EM. The evaluation design (benchmarking misalignment rates) is therefore covered.

### Domain
The domain is LLM safety and fine-tuning alignment. This is a well-established application area, as evidenced by [1], [2], [5], [6], and [7], all of which address emergent misalignment in LLMs during fine-tuning. While the specific instance (adaptive interleaving for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) is new, the general domain of LLM safety and alignment is not.
